title: Hyperthyroidism and Graves' disease (adult)
subject: endocrinology
summary: Confirm thyrotoxicosis and its cause (TRAb), control symptoms with a beta-blocker, treat Graves' disease with methimazole or carbimazole for 12 to 18 months (PTU before conception and in the first trimester) or with radioiodine or total thyroidectomy, and warn every patient to stop the drug and get an urgent blood count for fever or sore throat.

sections.title: Recognise and confirm
items: Symptoms: weight loss, heat intolerance, palpitations, tremor, anxiety, diarrhoea, oligomenorrhoea. Older people may present with atrial fibrillation, heart failure or apathy alone.
Thyrotoxicosis: suppressed TSH with raised FT4 and/or FT3 (T3 toxicosis: normal FT4, raised FT3). Subclinical hyperthyroidism: low TSH with normal FT4 and FT3.

Graves' disease: positive TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb), diffuse goitre, orbitopathy, pretibial myxoedema. Other causes: toxic multinodular goitre, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis (painless, postpartum, subacute), amiodarone, iodine excess, excess levothyroxine.
Fever, delirium, heart failure, jaundice or vomiting in a thyrotoxic patient suggests thyroid storm: treat as an emergency (see the thyroid storm protocol).

sections.title: Investigations
items: TSH first; if low, measure FT4 and FT3 on the same sample.
Measure TRAb to confirm Graves' disease. If TRAb is negative, a technetium scan separates toxic nodular disease (focal or patchy uptake) from thyroiditis (low uptake) (NICE).
Thyroid ultrasound if a nodule is palpable; colour Doppler ultrasound also supports a Graves' diagnosis (ETA).
Before starting an antithyroid drug: full blood count with differential and liver function tests.
ECG; in atrial fibrillation assess stroke risk and consider anticoagulation (warfarin or a DOAC).
Transient thyroiditis needs supportive treatment only (beta-blocker); antithyroid drugs do not help.

sections.title: Beta-blockade and antithyroid drugs
items: Beta-blocker for all suitable patients: propranolol 20 to 40 mg orally every 6 hours, or a longer-acting cardioselective agent (atenolol, bisoprolol). If beta-blockers are contraindicated, diltiazem or verapamil can control heart rate. Taper once euthyroid.

Methimazole or carbimazole is the drug of choice outside the first trimester. Start by severity: methimazole 10 to 30 mg once daily or carbimazole 15 to 40 mg/day (ETA). ATA doses methimazole by FT4: 1 to 1.5 times upper limit 5 to 10 mg, 1.5 to 2 times 10 to 20 mg, 2 to 3 times 30 to 40 mg.

Recheck FT4 and FT3 after 3 to 4 weeks (TSH stays suppressed for months) and titrate down to maintenance methimazole 2.5 to 10 mg/day. Block and replace (methimazole 30 mg/day plus levothyroxine) is an alternative outside pregnancy but does not improve remission.

Graves' disease: continue for 12 to 18 months, then measure TSH and TRAb and stop if both are normal. Persistently high TRAb: continue methimazole and recheck TRAb after 12 months, or choose radioiodine or surgery.
Relapse after a full course: radioiodine or total thyroidectomy is recommended; long-term low-dose methimazole is an acceptable alternative (ETA).

Propylthiouracil (PTU) is second line because of hepatotoxicity: use before conception and in the first trimester, or after minor reactions to methimazole. Dose 100 mg every 8 hours initially, maintenance 50 to 100 mg/day.
Minor rash or itch: antihistamine and continue. Agranulocytosis, hepatitis, vasculitis or a serious allergic reaction: stop and do not switch to the other thionamide; refer.

sections.title: Definitive treatment
items: Shared decision: ETA advises antithyroid drugs first in new Graves' disease; NICE offers radioiodine as first-line definitive treatment unless drugs are likely to achieve remission or radioiodine is unsuitable.

Radioiodine: contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding; postpone conception for at least 6 months afterwards (women and men). Pause antithyroid drugs about 1 week before and after. Most patients become hypothyroid and need lifelong levothyroxine.

Radioiodine can worsen orbitopathy: avoid it in moderate-to-severe or sight-threatening active disease; give oral prednisolone prophylaxis with mild active orbitopathy or risk factors (smoking, high TRAb, severe hyperthyroidism) (EUGOGO).

Total thyroidectomy by a high-volume surgeon for compressive goitre, suspected cancer, moderate-to-severe orbitopathy or patient preference. Make euthyroid with antithyroid drugs first; potassium iodide may be given for 10 days before surgery; correct vitamin D deficiency.
After total thyroidectomy start levothyroxine (1.6 mcg/kg/day) and monitor calcium for hypoparathyroidism.
Toxic nodular goitre or toxic adenoma rarely remits: radioiodine or surgery, or lifelong low-dose antithyroid drug if these are unsuitable (NICE).

sections.title: Monitoring
items: On antithyroid drugs: TSH, FT4 and FT3 every 6 weeks until TSH is in range, then TSH every 3 months until the drug is stopped (NICE).
Routine blood count and liver test monitoring is not useful because agranulocytosis is abrupt; test urgently if symptoms occur.
After stopping: TSH within 8 weeks, then every 3 months for a year, then yearly.
After radioiodine: TSH, FT4 and FT3 every 6 weeks for 6 months; start levothyroxine when hypothyroid; consider further treatment if still hyperthyroid at 6 months.

Subclinical hyperthyroidism: seek specialist advice if TSH is below 0.1 mIU/L on 2 readings 3 months apart with thyroid disease or symptoms; ETA recommends treatment over 65 with persistent TSH below 0.1 mIU/L.

sections.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
items: Aim for stable euthyroidism before conception. Switch methimazole or carbimazole to PTU when planning pregnancy or as soon as pregnancy is confirmed (methimazole embryopathy risk in weeks 6 to 10).

Women on low doses (methimazole below 5 to 10 mg/day or PTU below 50 to 100 mg/day) may stop the drug in early pregnancy, with thyroid tests every 2 weeks in the first trimester and every 4 weeks thereafter (ETA).

Use the lowest effective dose (starting PTU 50 to 200 mg/day by severity); avoid block and replace. Keep FT4 at or just above the upper limit of the reference range. Check FT4 and TSH every 2 weeks after starting, then every 4 weeks.
Consider switching PTU to methimazole if treatment is still needed after about 16 weeks (ETA).

Measure TRAb at booking in any woman with current or past Graves' disease (including after radioiodine or surgery); if raised, repeat at 18 to 22 weeks; above 3 times the cut-off, monitor the fetus for thyroid dysfunction.
Breastfeeding: methimazole is preferred (doses up to 20 mg/day are considered safe), taken after a feed. Relapse risk peaks 7 to 9 months postpartum.

sections.title: Orbitopathy and older adults
items: Ask about grittiness, diplopia, proptosis and reduced colour vision at each visit; refer urgently to ophthalmology for optic neuropathy or corneal exposure.
Stop smoking, restore and keep euthyroidism with antithyroid drugs, and consider selenium for 6 months in mild active orbitopathy (ETA, EUGOGO).

Older adults whose hyperthyroidism caused atrial fibrillation, heart failure or ischaemia should have definitive treatment, usually radioiodine; long-term low-dose methimazole suits older people with mild disease.
Carbimazole is the thionamide most widely prescribed in India; the same dosing principles apply.

sections.title: Refer urgently
items: Refer all new hyperthyroidism to endocrinology to plan definitive treatment.
Same-day review: suspected thyroid storm, atrial fibrillation with heart failure, or hyperthyroidism in pregnancy.
Urgent: agranulocytosis or hepatitis on an antithyroid drug; sight-threatening orbitopathy needs same-day ophthalmology.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Not warning the patient: fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers on an antithyroid drug means stop the drug and get an urgent full blood count (agranulocytosis, neutrophils below 0.5 x 10^9/L, usually within 3 months of starting). Give written advice.
Starting antithyroid drugs for painless, postpartum or subacute thyroiditis.
Titrating on TSH early in treatment instead of FT4 and FT3.
Giving radioiodine without confirming the patient is not pregnant or breastfeeding.
Continuing methimazole into early pregnancy in a woman trying to conceive.

drugs.name: Carbimazole
drugs.dose: 15 to 40 mg orally once daily initially by severity, then titrate to the lowest maintenance dose
drugs.notes: 12 to 18 months for Graves' disease. MHRA: effective contraception advised; risk of acute pancreatitis. Stop and check blood count for fever or sore throat.

drugs.name: Methimazole (thiamazole)
drugs.dose: 10 to 30 mg orally once daily initially (5 to 40 mg by FT4 severity); maintenance 2.5 to 10 mg once daily
drugs.notes: Drug of choice outside the first trimester and during breastfeeding.

drugs.name: Propylthiouracil (PTU)
drugs.dose: 100 mg orally every 8 hours initially; maintenance 50 to 100 mg/day in divided doses; in pregnancy start 50 to 200 mg/day by severity
drugs.notes: Preconception and first trimester, or thyroid storm. Hepatotoxicity; avoid in children.

drugs.name: Propranolol
drugs.notes: Symptom control until euthyroid; 40 mg four times daily also reduces T4 to T3 conversion. Avoid in asthma.

drugs.name: Prednisolone (radioiodine prophylaxis)
drugs.dose: 0.3 to 0.5 mg/kg/day orally, tapered and stopped over 3 months (higher risk); 0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg/day tapered over 6 weeks (lower risk)
drugs.notes: Mild active orbitopathy or risk factors for orbitopathy progression after radioiodine (EUGOGO 2021).

drugs.name: Levothyroxine (after ablation or total thyroidectomy)
drugs.dose: 1.6 mcg/kg/day orally once daily (25 to 50 mcg/day if older or cardiac)
drugs.notes: Also used with methimazole 30 mg/day in block and replace outside pregnancy.
